title: The centrosome is essentially a centre of force, not necessarily a material body

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The centrosome is essentially a centre of force, not necessarily a material body

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The centrosome is essentially a dynamic centre of force, which may or may not consist of a visible concentration of matter but tends to produce one, as shown by cells that live without visible centrosomes and centrosomes that disappear and form anew.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: We may safely take it that the centrosome, or the “attraction sphere,” is essentially a “centre of force,” and that this dynamic centre may or may not be constituted by (but will be very apt to produce) a concrete and visible concentration of matter.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Centrosome and cell surface”. Scope: centrosomes of animal and plant cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-17: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The observations motivating the claim are testable with open live imaging, but the ontological conclusion is not uniquely entailed. Existing data can resolve the functional core while leaving the historical force concept ambiguous.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track microtubule-organizing activity and centrosomal material through centrosome disappearance, ablation, or de novo assembly. The measurable core is supported if organizing activity can precede or persist without a visible body and subsequently recruits material.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Function without a canonical centrosome does not imply a disembodied force.

Absence of visible material depends on detection sensitivity.

A 'centre of force' is not uniquely defined in modern terms.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public images can test the empirical clause that a visible centrosome is not always present and can come and go. They cannot test the metaphysical clause that the centrosome is a force centre rather than matter, because sub-resolution material and a force centre look the same in those images. The resolvable part is the visibility pattern, not the nature of the centre.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score whether cells that divide and live lack a visible centrosome, and whether centrosomes disappear and reappear, versus a requirement for a persistent material body. Cycles of disappearance, and division without a visible centrosome, would support the visibility clause; a universal persistent particle would refute it. The further claim that the centrosome is essentially a centre of force is not separated by those observations.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Essentially a centre of force' does not specify a force to measure.

Plant spindles without centrioles still have microtubule-organising material.

A body below the resolution of the image is compatible with both a hidden particle and a pure force centre.
